story.headline: Gold sank about 3% to a one-year low under $3,900 as two Federal Reserve officials called for more rate hikes. The dollar still slipped, because a slide in tech shares pulled US bond yields lower.

reads.policy: Most central banks still lean toward higher rates because energy keeps inflation high. Two Fed officials called for more hikes, yet markets trimmed the odds of a December hike as tech shares fell, so the dollar's rate edge is wobbling. The Bank of Japan held but moved closer to a December hike.
reads.growth: The euro area grew faster than expected over the summer, but mostly thanks to Ireland, with France shrinking and Italy flat. Canada's economy has stalled since before its rate hike, which weakens the case for another. US business activity is cooling a little from a fast pace.
reads.inflation: Energy keeps prices high nearly everywhere, but unevenly: inflation cooled in Germany while it jumped in Italy and France. US wage growth held steady, so pay is not adding fresh pressure. Japan's central bank says underlying inflation has reached its goal.
reads.risk: A slide in big tech shares over AI spending sent money into US government bonds and the safe-haven currencies. That pulled US yields down, so the dollar slipped even as investors grew nervous. Gold got no safety boost and fell as some investors sold it to cover losses.
reads.tot: Oil stayed high as fear of new US strikes on Iran outweighed a recovery in Gulf exports. That keeps helping exporters like Canada and Australia and costing importers like Japan and the euro area.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, and the loonie's climb since Canada's rate hike puts those bets under pressure. Their bets against the euro are the largest in years, so good euro news could force them to buy it back. Their big bets on gold are losing money as it slides.
reads.fiscal: France's budget fight is still unresolved and keeps a weight on the euro, with a vote on taxes due November 3. France's economy shrank over the summer, which makes its deficit harder to close. The UK Budget passed calmly, so the pound is trading on rates, not borrowing.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and on October 30 two more officials called for further hikes. Markets still see a December hike as likely, though a slide in tech shares has trimmed the odds.
fed.priced: December: hike likely, though less certain than right after the meeting.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal on high energy prices, and the economy is still growing fast.
fed.watch: The October jobs report next week and the tech share slide: strong hiring would firm up a December hike, a deeper sell-off would loosen it.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% on October 28, its first hike since 2023, and said more may be needed. But the economy did not grow in July or August, which makes a second hike soon harder to justify.
boc.priced: December: another hike possible, a bit less than even odds.
boc.why: Energy has lifted Canadian inflation and the bank raised its forecasts sharply, but growth is running well below what it expected.
boc.watch: Canadian job and inflation figures before the December 9 decision, and oil prices.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised by holding at 2.75% on October 28, but it says more tightening is likely. That makes December a live meeting and limits the kiwi's fall.
rbnz.priced: December: a hike possible; no firm odds yet.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the 1–3% target, and firms say they plan to raise prices more.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand job and price figures before the December 9 decision, and anything Governor Anna Breman says about timing.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% on October 29, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. Hot inflation in Italy and France backs that, while cooler prices in Germany soften it.
ecb.why: Energy costs have pushed euro-area inflation well above the 2% goal, and the economy grew faster than expected over the summer.
ecb.watch: Euro-area inflation for October at 4:00 AM CT on Wednesday, November 4, and whether worries over French government debt return.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on October 30, with one member voting to hike, and said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. Governor Kazuo Ueda named no date, but a December hike looks likely and would give the yen some support.
boj.why: The bank judges inflation to be running at its goal, with prices rising beyond energy and the jobs market tight.
boj.watch: Japanese wage and price figures and any move by Tokyo to buy yen; the next decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3 after inflation ran hotter than it forecast. That supports the Aussie.
rba.why: Underlying inflation is running above the bank's own forecasts, and business-level prices are still climbing.
rba.watch: China's factory surveys at 8:30 PM CT Friday, then the decision at 9:30 PM CT on Monday, November 2.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates on November 5, and the debate is already about December. Firms now expect faster price rises, which makes the hike easier to justify.
boe.priced: November: hike all but certain; December: a second hike possible.
boe.why: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, driven by energy and fuel, with service prices still sticky.
boe.watch: The decision at 6:00 AM CT on Thursday, November 5, and whether the bank hints at a second hike in December.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and has said it is less ready to fight a weaker franc. Swiss inflation is low, so the franc mostly moves on global fear and calm, and it firmed as tech shares slid.
snb.priced: December: markets split; no move is the slight favourite.
snb.why: Inflation is below target, so the bank has no reason to raise rates while others do.
snb.watch: Swiss inflation figures next week and the global mood; the next decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits near the top of the board because the Federal Reserve is still expected to raise rates in December and US inflation runs hot. Falling US yields during a tech share slide have taken some of that edge away.

notes.policy: The Fed's next move still looks like a hike, likely in December, and two officials called for more on October 30, which keeps US rates high.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running well above the Fed's goal, mostly on fuel, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: growth is slowing, energy imports cost more, and France's budget fight weighs on it. The European Central Bank still leans toward a hike in December, which gives it some support.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank held in October and points to a hike in December, so it lags banks that are moving sooner.
notes.growth: Euro-area growth beat forecasts over the summer only thanks to Ireland; France shrank, Italy stalled and business surveys keep missing.
notes.inflation: Prices are rising fast in Italy, France and the supply chain, which keeps pressure on the European Central Bank to hike, even as Germany cooled.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so high oil drains money out.
notes.positioning: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could force them to buy it back.
notes.fiscal: France's unresolved budget and heavy debt keep investors wary of euro-area bonds.

GBP.summary: The pound scores well because the Bank of England is almost certain to raise rates in November, inflation is high and the economy is holding up. It is at its strongest against the euro this year.

notes.policy: The Bank of England is expected to raise rates on November 5, among the most likely hikes of any major bank.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been stronger than expected, even though shoppers are gloomy.
notes.inflation: UK inflation rose to its highest in about a year, which keeps the Bank of England leaning toward hikes.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below other major economies' and high oil costs Japan money. The Bank of Japan now says inflation has reached its goal, so a December hike could start to change that.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan held in October and its rate is still far below others', though it says inflation has reached its goal, which points to a December hike.
notes.risk: The yen gains when investors look for safety, as when tech shares fell, and Tokyo's warnings limit how weak it gets.
notes.tot: Japan imports almost all its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates, but the franc still draws money when markets get nervous.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is below target, which keeps the Swiss National Bank from raising rates.
notes.risk: The franc tends to gain when investors look for safety, and it firmed as tech shares slid.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well because the Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates in November and high commodity prices bring money in. A weakening job market is the main drag.

notes.policy: The Reserve Bank of Australia is expected to raise rates on November 3, which supports the Aussie.
notes.growth: Business surveys slipped into decline in October and unemployment is at a five-year high.
notes.inflation: Underlying inflation ran hotter than the bank expected, and business prices are still climbing, which keeps hikes coming.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and resources abroad, so high prices bring money into the country.

CAD.summary: The loonie scores well now that the Bank of Canada has started raising rates and high oil prices bring money in. Growth is the soft spot: the economy has stalled.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and may do so again in December, which narrows the gap with US rates.
notes.growth: Canada's economy did not grow in July or August, well short of what the Bank of Canada expected.
notes.inflation: Producer and raw-material prices are rising fast, which keeps the Bank of Canada leaning toward more hikes.
notes.tot: Canada is a big oil exporter, so high crude prices bring money into the country.

NZD.summary: The kiwi fell after New Zealand's central bank held rates when markets expected a hike, but the bank still expects to tighten later. A steady economy and firm export prices limit the damage.

notes.growth: New Zealand's services sector keeps growing, and business confidence rose in October.
notes.risk: The kiwi has held steady through the stock slide, a sign investors are not rushing out of it.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
